KEY MESSAGE 1...
As of 1:24 PM EST...The surface high pressure has moved east 
offshore into the Atlantic, with an axis of upper-level ridging 
positioned just to the west of eastern New York and western New 
England. This ridging continues to bring above normal 
temperatures this afternoon, ranging from the upper 50s and 
lower 60s in higher terrain and nearly reaching 70 degrees in 
the Mid-Hudson Valley. Moisture has been steadily increasing 
throughout the day, with ensemble anomalies for precipitable 
water values reaching +2 to +3 STDEV above normal into tonight. 
Radar has showed some light showers over the northern 
Adirondacks throughout the late morning and early afternoon 
today, which likely are forming due to upsloping as there is 
minimal forcing at this time. Much of this rain may not be 
reaching the ground, as observations are barely reaching 0.05 
inches across a few sites in the northern Adirondacks. 
Temperatures overnight will remain mild, only dropping into the 
mid 40s to lower 50s. There is potential for some patchy 
fog/mist to develop overnight in the Mid-Hudson Valley as 
dewpoints increase and skies partially clear.

The aforementioned axis of an upper-level ridge will move 
directly overhead tomorrow, bringing the highest temperatures of
the week. Current guidance continues to show 850 mb ensemble 
anomalies reaching +1 to +2 STDEV above normal and 850 mb 
temperatures ranging from about 12 to 15 degrees C. High 
temperatures are expected to reach into the lower to mid 70s in 
our valley regions tomorrow, while higher terrain will see 
temperatures more in the upper 60s. Southerly flow will persist 
throughout the day and advect in more moisture, allowing dew 
points to gradually rise. Breezier conditions are also expected,
with wind gusts up to 10-15 kts in the afternoon and evening, 
particularly in the N/S oriented valleys.

KEY MESSAGE 2...

A low pressure system tracks from the Great Lakes Region into 
southeast Canada Wed night into Thu morning, as a cold front 
approaches from the west. The cold front brings a round of 
showers to the region initially before daybreak to the 
west/southwest Adirondacks and the western Mohawk Valley, and 
then across the rest of eastern NY into western New England in 
the late morning through the afternoon. PWATS rise to 1 to 3 
STDEVs above normal based on latest NAEFS with the actual values
1-1.5". The low-level convergence increases along the front for
the showers. It will become breezy. The better upper level 
forcing is west of the Hudson River Valley. The latest 24-hr NBM
probabilities >0.25" rainfall are in the 60-95% range for the 
period ending 06Z/1 AM Fri are situated across the 
west/southwest Adirondacks, eastern Catskills, western Mohawk 
Valley and the southern Greens. Probabilities are generally 
20-50% for rest of the region with the lowest south and east of 
the Capital District. The probs remain high in the 50-60% range
for greater than 0.50" rainfall for the same 24-hr time frame 
ending 06Z/1 am Fri for the west/southwest Adirondacks. Most 
locations will receive about a tenth of an inch of rain, which 
will be the most widespread measurable rainfall in close to 20 
days for the region. Low temps will be Wed night in the upper 
40s to mid 50s. Max temps on Thu will still run above normal in 
the mid 60s to around 70F in the valleys and upper 50s to 
lower/mid 60s over the higher terrain. 

The initial cold front settles south of the region and stalls
with some light showers Thu night early on, as a positively-
tilted mid and upper level trough sets-up over the Midwest and 
Great Lakes Region. A wave of low pressure develops along the 
frontal boundary south of the region and potentially brings 
additional periods of rain Fri-Fri night. The location of the 
front and the track of the wave still show some variability 
based on the medium range guidance and ensembles. The latest NBM
has 24-hr probabilities > 1" of rain by 12Z/7 am Sat in the 
40-60% range across most of western New England, the southern 
Taconics and the mid Hudson Valley. The highest probs are over 
Litchfield County, CT and near I-84. Lighter amounts are 
possible north and west. The track of the wave will make the 
difference where moderate to locally heavy rainfall falls. The
rain will be beneficial due to the recent dry spell and hydro 
issues are not anticipated at this time. Friday will be the last
day of temps about 10 degrees above normal with highs in the 
mid 50s to mid/upper 60s.

A closed/cutoff upper low looks to settle over NY and New 
England for scattered showers and cool conditions for the 
weekend based on the NBM/ensembles and medium range 
deterministic guidance. Temps trend near to slightly below 
normal for the close of the weekend. The cooler and unsettled 
weather looks to continue into early next week.
